narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of afro-textured hair, was likely worn by many, as it was a defining feature of African-American culture during this time period. Cornrows, also known as three-strand braids, were a traditional style that originated from Africa and continued to be practiced in the African diaspora. The concept of protective hairstyles, designed to minimize manipulation and exposure of hair to environmental elements, may have been understood and implemented by women, although specific documentation from this era is limited. It's worth noting that the 1950s were a time before the natural hair movement, which emerged in the 1960s, and therefore we can only speculate on how hairstyles were perceived during this decade. Nonetheless, it is clear that Black and African women's hair was a vital aspect of their cultural identity, with various styles serving as expressions of heritage and self-expression.
